summary: Defines the Host Resources MIB for managing host computers, covering things such as storage, processes and installed software. It clarifies the earlier version based on implementation experience and moves to the SMIv2 format. It is a standards-track document at the draft standard level.

plainLanguage.summary: This document defines a standard set of questions a management system can ask about a computer: how much memory it has, what disks and devices are attached, which programs are running, and what software is installed. Every host can answer them the same way, whatever its operating system.

subtitle: A standard SNMP MIB for asking a computer about its memory, disks, devices, running programs and installed software.

tldr.problem: Each vendor's machines exposed their own measurements, so a management system could not ask a workstation or a server the same questions and get comparable answers.
tldr.mechanism: The document defines a MIB module of objects that every host can implement: system state, storage, devices, the software currently running, and the software installed. It is written in SMIv2, and a translation back to the older SMIv1 produces the same meaning.
tldr.outcome: A management station can take an inventory of a host's hardware and software, watch its processors, storage and printers, and see which programs are running and how much memory each is using, without knowing what operating system is underneath.

today: RFC 2790 is a Draft Standard from March 2000 that obsoletes RFC 1514, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It documents the Host Resources MIB in SMIv2 format while remaining semantically identical to the SMIv1-based MIB it replaces.

sections.title: The SNMP Framework and What This MIB Adds
sections.content:
The SNMP network management framework consists of five major components: an overall architecture; the mechanisms for describing and naming objects and events, where the first version is SMIv1 and the second is SMIv2; the message protocols for transferring management information, SNMPv1, SNMPv2c and SNMPv3; the protocol operations for accessing managed information; and a set of fundamental applications together with the view-based access control mechanism.

Managed objects are accessed through a virtual information store, the Management Information Base, and objects in the MIB are defined using the mechanisms of the SMI. This memo specifies a MIB module that is compliant to SMIv2. A MIB conforming to SMIv1 can be produced through the appropriate translations, and the resulting translated MIB must be semantically equivalent, except where objects or events are omitted because no translation is possible, which is the case with Counter64. Some machine readable information in SMIv2 is converted into textual descriptions in SMIv1 during translation, but that loss of machine readable information is not considered to change the semantics of the MIB.

The memo obsoletes RFC 1514, the earlier Host Resources MIB. It extends that specification by clarifying changes based on implementation and deployment experience and by documenting the MIB in SMIv2 format while remaining semantically identical to the existing SMIv1-based MIB. The revision notes list what changed: a copyright notice, an updated introduction to the SNMP framework, an updated references section, a reference to RFC 2119 and a meaningful security considerations section; a new IANA considerations section for the registration of new types; conversion to the new SMIv2 syntax for a list of types and macros; the use of new textual conventions including TruthValue, DateAndTime, AutonomousType and InterfaceIndexOrZero; a typo fix in hrPrinterStatus; missing error bits added to hrPrinterDetectedErrorState; a clarification that the size of objects of type InternationalDisplayString is a number of octets rather than encoded symbols; and clarifications of the use of a list of objects based on implementation experience.
sections.plainLanguage: The SNMP framework is the machinery for naming and reading managed objects. This document is one MIB module within it, rewritten in the newer SMIv2 notation while keeping the same meaning as the 1993 version it replaces.

sections.title: What the Host Resources MIB Covers
sections.content:
The Host Resources MIB defines a uniform set of objects useful for the management of host computers. Host computers are independent of the operating system, the network services, or any software application. The MIB defines objects which are common across many computer system architectures.

The term host is construed to mean any computer that communicates with other similar computers attached to the Internet and that is directly used by one or more human beings. Although the MIB does not necessarily apply to devices whose primary function is communications services, such as terminal servers, routers, bridges or monitoring equipment, such relevance is not explicitly precluded. The MIB instruments attributes common to all Internet hosts, including for example both personal computers and systems that run variants of Unix.

There are also objects in the SNMPv2-MIB and the IF-MIB which provide host management functionality, and implementation of the System and Interfaces groups is mandatory for implementors of the Host Resources MIB. The module is rooted at mib-2 25, named host, with six subtrees: the system group at 1, the storage group at 2, the device group at 3, the running software group at 4, the running software performance group at 5, and the installed software group at 6, plus an administrative subtree at 7 that holds the conformance statements and the types module.
sections.plainLanguage: The MIB covers anything a person sits at and uses, not just servers, and it is written so that the same questions work whatever operating system is underneath. The System group from the older MIB-II and the Interfaces group are mandatory as well.

sections.title: The System and Storage Groups
sections.content:
The system group holds the objects that apply to the host as a whole. hrSystemUptime is the amount of time since the host was last initialised, which is different from sysUpTime in the SNMPv2-MIB because that is the uptime of the network management portion of the system. hrSystemDate is the host's notion of the local date and time of day, and is writable. hrSystemInitialLoadDevice is the index of the device entry for the device the host is configured to load its initial operating system configuration from, and hrSystemInitialLoadParameters holds the parameters supplied to that device; writing to either only changes the configuration used the next time the operating system is loaded and does not cause a reload. hrSystemNumUsers counts the user sessions for which the host is storing state, and hrSystemProcesses counts the process contexts currently loaded or running. hrSystemMaxProcesses is the maximum number of process contexts the system can support, and is zero if there is no fixed maximum; on systems that do have one it helps diagnose failures that occur when the maximum is reached.

The storage group starts with hrMemorySize, the amount of physical read-write main memory, typically RAM, contained by the host, measured in kilobytes. The storage table then has one entry per storage area, holding its type, a description, the size of its allocation units, its total size, the amount used, and the number of allocation failures. The storage types are registered separately and include other, RAM, virtual memory, fixed disk, removable disk and floppy disk, and more may be added over time.
sections.plainLanguage: The system group answers questions about the machine as a whole: how long it has been up, what its clock says, how many users and processes it has, and where it boots from. The storage group answers how much memory it has and how each storage area is being used.

sections.title: The Device Group
sections.content:
The device group starts with a table whose entries describe the devices attached to the host. Each entry carries a device type, a description, an identifier, a status and an error count. The status values are unknown, running, warning, testing and down, and the meanings are spelled out: running means the device is up and no unusual error conditions are known, and the other values describe the states the agent cannot rule out.

The device type tells a manager where the detail is. If the type is a processor there is a matching entry in the processor table, if it is a network device there is one in the network table, if it is a printer there is one in the printer table, and if it is disk storage there is one in the disk storage table.

The processor table carries the firmware identification of the processor and its load, which is the average over the last minute of the percentage of time that the processor was not idle; implementations may approximate the one-minute smoothing period if necessary. The network table records the interface index of the network device. The printer table carries the printer status and the detected error state, and the error state was extended with missing error bits in this revision. The disk storage table records whether the media is accessible, what it is, whether it is removable and its capacity in kilobytes, where a value of zero is used when removable media is currently removed. The partition table records the partitions found on the disks, with their label, identifier, size and the index of the file system mounted on them, and the file system table records the mount point, the remote mount point, the type, the access, whether the file system is bootable, the storage it sits on, and the dates of the last full and last partial backup.
sections.plainLanguage: Every attached device gets a row with a type, a status and an error count, and the type points at a second table with the details: processor load, the network interface index, printer status, disk media and capacity, partitions and mounted file systems.

sections.title: Running and Installed Software
sections.content:
The running software group has one entry for each program currently running on the host, holding the index, the name of the program, its identifier, the path it was started from, the parameters it was given, its type and its status. The running software performance group augments those entries with two measurements: the number of centi-seconds of the total system's CPU resources consumed by the process, which on a multi-processor system may increment by more than one centi-second in one centi-second of real time, and the total amount of real system memory allocated to the process, measured in kilobytes.

The installed software group holds the software installed in long-term storage on the host, such as a disk drive, and does not include software loadable remotely from a network server. Different implementations track software in varying ways: some track executable files as distinct pieces of software, others track packages of related files, or system and application patches. The table is useful for identifying and inventorying software on a host and for diagnosing incompatibility and version mismatch problems between pieces of hardware and software. Because the table is likely to contain many entries, an object records the value of sysUpTime when an entry was last added, renamed or deleted, so that a management station can tell when re-reading the table might be worthwhile, and another records the time of the last update of the whole table.
sections.plainLanguage: One table lists the programs running now, with how much processor time and how much memory each is using. Another lists the software installed on disk, so that a manager can build an inventory and spot version mismatches.

sections.title: Type Definitions and IANA Registration
sections.content:
The document contains type definitions for storage types, device types and file system types, for use as the values of hrStorageType, hrDeviceType and hrFSType. As new computing technologies are developed, new types need to be registered, and IANA is designated as the registration authority for registrations beyond those published in the document. IANA maintains the HOST-RESOURCES-TYPES module as new registrations are added and publishes new versions of it. After the initial revision, this module is maintained by IANA.

Given the large number of such technologies and the potential confusion in naming them, such as a technology known by two names or by a name and an acronym, there is a real danger that more than one registration might be created for what is essentially the same technology. To ensure that future type registrations are performed correctly, applications for new types are reviewed by a Designated Expert appointed by the IESG.
sections.plainLanguage: The list of storage types, device types and file system types is kept in a separate module that IANA maintains, so that new kinds of hardware can be added over time. Because the same thing often has two names, an expert reviews each new registration to make sure it is not a duplicate.

sections.title: Internationalization Considerations
sections.content:
The MIB has many objects that identify file-system pathnames on the managed host. Many file systems allow pathnames to be encoded in a variety of character sets other than ASCII, but do not support the encoding of the actual character set used with the pathname. The implementation strategy is that user interfaces, such as character-based shells or graphical applications, have configuration options that control with which character set they interpret and display all pathnames. This is often a per-user configuration, so that users using different languages and character sets on a multi-user system may each work effectively with their preferred character set, and a human usually controls this configuration. If an application is not configured, or is configured incorrectly, it will often have trouble displaying pathnames in the intended character set.

This made it important for the MIB to handle two issues: pathname objects must be able to transfer a variety of character sets with potentially multi-byte encodings, and host agents will generally not be correctly configured for the appropriate character set to be used for all files on the system, particularly on a system with multiple users using different character sets, so it was impossible to mandate that the agent tag pathnames with the character set in use. Both issues were solved with the introduction of the InternationalDisplayString textual convention, which supports multi-byte encodings. Network management stations should use a local algorithm to determine which character set is in use and how it should be displayed, and it is expected that station applications will rely on human configuration to choose the character set in which to interpret InternationalDisplayString objects, much like an application running locally on that host.
sections.plainLanguage: File names can be written in many character sets, and the agent usually does not know which one a given file uses. So pathnames are sent as raw octets and the management station works out the character set locally, the same way a program running on the host would.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A number of management objects defined in this MIB have a MAX-ACCESS clause of read-write. Such objects may be considered sensitive or vulnerable in some network environments, and support for SET operations in a non-secure environment without proper protection can have a negative effect on system operations.

A number of managed objects in the MIB may also contain sensitive information. The objects in the Running Software Group list information about running software on the system, including the operating system software and version, and some may wish not to disclose to others what software they are running. An inventory of the running software and versions may also help an attacker who hopes to exploit software bugs in certain applications, and the same issues exist for the objects in the Installed Software Group. It is therefore important to control even GET access to these objects, and possibly to encrypt the values of these objects when sending them over the network, though not all versions of SNMP provide features for such a secure environment.

SNMPv1 by itself is not a secure environment, and even if the network itself is secure, for example by using IPSec, there is still no control over who on that network may GET or SET the objects in this MIB. The memo recommends that implementers consider the security features provided by the SNMPv3 framework, specifically the User-based Security Model of RFC 2574 and the View-based Access Control Model of RFC 2575. It is then the customer or user responsibility to ensure that the SNMP entity giving access to an instance of this MIB is properly configured to give access only to those principals that have legitimate rights to read or change them.
sections.plainLanguage: Some of these objects can be changed, and others, such as the list of software versions, tell an attacker what to attack. The memo therefore asks for SNMPv3 with user-based security and view-based access control, and leaves it to the operator to give access only to the people who should have it.

items.title: hrSystemUptime
items.text: Time since the host was last initialised, which is not the same as the uptime of its management part.

items.title: hrSystemDate
items.text: The host's own idea of the local date and time of day. Writable.

items.title: hrSystemInitialLoadDevice
items.text: The device the host boots from. Writing changes the next boot, not the current one.

items.title: hrSystemNumUsers
items.text: The number of user sessions the host is keeping state for.

items.title: hrSystemProcesses
items.text: The number of process contexts currently loaded or running.

items.title: hrSystemMaxProcesses
items.text: The maximum number of process contexts the system supports, or zero if there is no fixed limit.

items.title: hrMemorySize
items.text: The amount of physical read-write main memory in the host, in kilobytes.

items.text: Applications for new types are reviewed by a Designated Expert appointed by the IESG.

items.title: Why the review
items.text: The same technology often has two names, so without a check more than one registration could be created for what is really the same thing.

viz.caption: What the memo asks operators to do

items.title: Writable objects are sensitive
items.text: Objects with read-write access may be vulnerable, and allowing SET operations without protection can hurt the running system.

items.title: Version lists help an attacker
items.text: The running and installed software groups disclose the operating system and application versions, which point straight at known bugs.

items.title: Control reads too
items.text: It is important to control even GET access to those objects, and possibly to encrypt their values on the way across the network.

items.title: Use SNMPv3
items.text: The memo recommends the User-based Security Model and the View-based Access Control Model, and leaves the operator to grant access only to the right users.
